messages.subject_clean: Conversion of Critical Leaf Water Threshold and estimation of other Vegetation Parameters (micro_ncep)
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm working on fine tuning a model to estimate air temp, soil temp, and relative humidity in a deciduous forest. Overall, the correlations are mediocre except for relative humidity which is quite poor. To try and combat this I am trying to accurately parameterize the soil moisture/evapotranspiration parameters. Unfortunately, I am not a botanist and am wading into unfamiliar territory when it comes to vegetation parameters. As result, I have a few questions...

What are the default parameter values related to vegetation based on in the soil moisture mode?

How do I/is it possible to convert critical leaf water potential from pressure (bars) to thermal heat capacity used by the model?

Is there a database that describes values for these parameters broken down by general vegetation class? (Parameters: including R1, RW, & RL)

Best,
Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

Those soil moisture plant parameters are taken straight out of
Campbell, G.S. (1985) Soil Physics with Basic: Transport Models for Soil-Plant Systems.

and there's a modern version of that book:
Bittelli, M., Campbell, G.S. & Tomei, F. (2015) Soil Physics with Python: Transport in the Soil–Plant–Atmosphere System, Oxford University Press, Oxford.

Re getting the humidity right - is this humidity near the ground? There's no influence of the soil moisture model on humidity near the ground - that is simply based on the reference height humidity and air temperature and adjusting the humidity near the ground for the calculated air temperature near the ground. Ilya Maclean has been developing a model of conditions under the canopy so he might be able to make suggestions.

I'm not sure I understand your question about converting leaf water potential to thermal heat capacity.

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

Yes microclimc is the package Ilya is working on - I'm not sure if it will help with the humidity issue.

Re water potential units, J/kg = kPa = bar/100,  whereas thermal specific heat capacity is J/kg/C. Water potential is energy per unit mass or volume in comparison to pure water. If you assume that water has a density of 1000 kg / m3, then you get the equivalence of J/kg and kPa.

All the best,
Mike

I want to calculate multiple variables from the ectotherm subroutine for 200 geographic points (where shade % varies for each one).
To achieve it, I need to run micro_ncep and ectotherm for each element of a list of locations (each with a different value of minshade and maxshade), as well as save the corresponding micro and ecto in a successive list of objects.
Have any of you done something similar? and if this is the case, would you please share the script with me to give me an idea of how I should do it?

Thank you very much in advance.

messages.subject: Re: run micro_ncep and ectotherm for several geographic points
messages.subject_clean: run micro_ncep and ectotherm for several geographic points
messages.body_plain:
Hi Israel,

I think you just need a loop 'for' to go through each of your coordinates. You could try something like this:

data <- read.csv("your_data.csv", header = T)

for(i in 1:nrow(data)){

micro <- micro_nceploc = c(data$long[i], data$lat[i]),  # coordinates
                        minshade= data$shade[i], maxshade= data$shade[i],  #the columns in your dataset with the % of shade
                        runshade=1
                        )

ecto <- ectotherm()

environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
output <- data.frame(meanTC = NA)     # dataframe to store what you are interested in
output$meanTC <- mean(environ$TC)  # example of variable from the ectotherm model

if(i == 1){
    output.frame <- output

  }else{
    output.frame <- rbind(output.frame, output)
  }
}

Hope this can help,

Cheers,
Rudi

messages.subject_clean: Effective shade values for small animals in the undergrowth (micro_ncep)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike (and all),

Edited:

Thanks for your responses and suggestions.

I would like to also use the soil moisture model. However, the wetland sites I sampled are sphagnum peat bogs, so with organic rather than mineral soils. These I understand are likely to have low mineral content (primarily silicate), low thermal conductivity and very low bulk densities. Given this, would it be expected that the models would work just as well for these?

If so, in the context of a sphagnum peat bog, am I correct in interpreting the inputs as follows:

Thcond = x, Soil minerals thermal conductivity (W/mK) --> thermal conductivity of silicate (presuming this to be the primary mineral)
Density = x, Soil minerals density (Mg/m3) --> the inorganic ('ash') content of the soil
SpecHeat = x, Soil minerals specific heat (J/kg-K) --> again of silicate?
BulkDensity = x, Soil bulk density (Mg/m3)  --> have lit values for sphagnum bog.

Alternatively, I have also been able to find values for the thermal conductivity (and specific heat) of dried sphagnum moss peat soils. But i'm not sure if these could be used in place of the first three inputs?

Many thanks.

Tom

On Thursday, April 16, 2020 at 10:24:45 AM UTC+10 Michael Kearney wrote:
> Hi Tom,
>
> I've got them calling in the park opposite my house.
>
> That plan sounds sensible - I'd play around with different shade constraints and see what happens. Different ponds will have different amounts of shade, from a bare farm dam at one extreme to one surrounded by think veg at the other. You were referring to shade as fractional in your question, but it is in units of % for the model input - just checking that you're aware of this. You could set the parameter 'shdburrow' to 2, so they are always retreating in the shade and you could play with either limiting the minimum depth they can retreat to or let them go as deep as they need to avoid temperature extremes, so you can assess if they need access to deep cracks at certain times of the year.
>
> You're correct that the reference temperature will not be affected by shade - it is simply an hourly interpolation of the weather station input data (as is the reference wind speed and humidity) - a non-microclimate variable though it can be used to estimate the temperature an animal would be exposed to if it climbed high off the ground and out of the boundary layer.
>
> Note that if you run the soil moisture model, set the soil properties to clay, and put a multiplier on the rainfall (the 'rainmult' parameter) to account for a catchment, you can do a pretty good prediction of a wetland. Check the 'POOLDEP' output in metout to see what the estimated depth of water pooling on the surface is. This will also cause the soil to become waterlogged for more of the year, and may better capture the microclimate that C. signifera experiences by hanging around wetlands.
>
> All the best,
> Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

Probably the thermal conditions in those peat bogs are driven by the moisture content more than anything. You can try and make the thermal properties of the soil close to peat. Note that you're specifying the solid non-water thermal components of the soil, and the overall thermal properties of the soil are then finally determined by the model from the relative amount of air, water and 'soil minerals'. There are values for organic material in Campbell and Norman 1998 Table 8.2:

Density: 1.3 Mg/m3
Spec. heat: 1920 J/kg-K
Thermal cond: 0.25 W/m-K

But you might also want to play around with the rainmult parameter to simulate a kind of catchment effect concentrating the rain if it is a little wetland - if you add deeper clay layers you can end up with quite a good simulation of a wetland.

But, as always, the main thing is to have good quality microclimatic data to compare with.

All the best,
Mike

On Friday, October 16, 2020 at 10:11:06 AM UTC+11 bur...@deakin.edu.au wrote:
> Hi Mike (and all),
>
> Edited:
>
> Thanks for your responses and suggestions.
>
> I would like to also use the soil moisture model. However, the wetland sites I sampled are sphagnum peat bogs, so with organic rather than mineral soils. These I understand are likely to have low mineral content (primarily silicate), low thermal conductivity and very low bulk densities. Given this, would it be expected that the models would work just as well for these?
>
> If so, in the context of a sphagnum peat bog, am I correct in interpreting the inputs as follows:
>
> Thcond = x, Soil minerals thermal conductivity (W/mK) --> thermal conductivity of silicate (presuming this to be the primary mineral)
> Density = x, Soil minerals density (Mg/m3) --> the inorganic ('ash') content of the soil
> SpecHeat = x, Soil minerals specific heat (J/kg-K) --> again of silicate?
> BulkDensity = x, Soil bulk density (Mg/m3)  --> have lit values for sphagnum bog.
>
> Alternatively, I have also been able to find values for the thermal conductivity (and specific heat) of dried sphagnum moss peat soils. But i'm not sure if these could be used in place of the first three inputs?
>
> Many thanks.
>
> Tom
>
> On Thursday, April 16, 2020 at 10:24:45 AM UTC+10 Michael Kearney wrote:
> > Hi Tom,
> >
> > I've got them calling in the park opposite my house.
> >
> > That plan sounds sensible - I'd play around with different shade constraints and see what happens. Different ponds will have different amounts of shade, from a bare farm dam at one extreme to one surrounded by think veg at the other. You were referring to shade as fractional in your question, but it is in units of % for the model input - just checking that you're aware of this. You could set the parameter 'shdburrow' to 2, so they are always retreating in the shade and you could play with either limiting the minimum depth they can retreat to or let them go as deep as they need to avoid temperature extremes, so you can assess if they need access to deep cracks at certain times of the year.
> >
> > You're correct that the reference temperature will not be affected by shade - it is simply an hourly interpolation of the weather station input data (as is the reference wind speed and humidity) - a non-microclimate variable though it can be used to estimate the temperature an animal would be exposed to if it climbed high off the ground and out of the boundary layer.
> >
> > Note that if you run the soil moisture model, set the soil properties to clay, and put a multiplier on the rainfall (the 'rainmult' parameter) to account for a catchment, you can do a pretty good prediction of a wetland. Check the 'POOLDEP' output in metout to see what the estimated depth of water pooling on the surface is. This will also cause the soil to become waterlogged for more of the year, and may better capture the microclimate that C. signifera experiences by hanging around wetlands.
> >
> > All the best,
> > Mike
